messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rafael had spent most of his adult life in uniform, and at 55 he still carried himself like a Navy officer even off duty: measured, upright, watchful. But in the war zone where he had been assigned as a civilian adviser years earlier, those habits had not protected him from what happened on a narrow street outside a clinic after a sudden explosion tore through a crowd gathered for medicine and food. He had been close enough to smell the dust and burned fuel, close enough to hear people calling for children, and close enough to see the confusion that followed when the wounded could not be moved quickly. What stayed with Rafael was not only the violence of that moment but the feeling that he had failed in some basic human duty. He had come to believe he was a weak person, that he should have protected others and did not, and that he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened. Those convictions settled over him and, over time, shaped the way the event lived in his mind.

When the memory returned, it did not arrive as a simple recollection. It came back with the same heat, the same metallic smell, the same cries and dust, as if the scene were happening again in front of him. At other times he could call up the facts in a flat, numb way, but even then the distance felt disturbing, as though he were describing something that happened to a stranger rather than to a man who had stood there and done too little. He was often caught between those two forms of remembering: one that flooded him with guilt and made the whole moment feel completely real across all his senses at once, and another that left him strangely empty, which in its own way felt like another sign of weakness. The more he revisited the scene in his mind, the more those appraisals hardened. Each time he remembered the crowd, the cries, and his own paralysis, the old judgment returned with greater force: he had failed to protect others, and that failure proved what kind of man he was.

That was how the loop began to take hold in daily life. Rafael worked as a Navy Officer in a support role that kept him around radios, incident reports, and briefings, and there were moments at work that would jolt the memory loose—a sudden alarm tone, a loud bang from a dropped tool in the corridor, or the sight of a crowded intake area on a ship or base that echoed the chaos of the clinic street. When that happened, the scene would surge in with such vividness that he could feel the heat on his skin and hear the voices as if they were beside him. Afterwards he would tell himself again that he was weak, that a stronger man would have acted, that he had no right to call himself protective or competent. Those thoughts did not calm him; they drew him back to the event, and the more he replayed it, the more real and humiliating it became, as if every sensory detail were evidence against him. Even when he could only recall it in a blank, detached way, the numbness itself fed the same conclusion: something was wrong with him, and it must mean he had failed in a deeper sense.

Over the years he began arranging his life around the fear of being pulled into that scene again. He stayed busy with paperwork, kept conversations practical, and avoided talking about the war zone with colleagues or with the partner he lived with, because saying it aloud seemed to risk opening the door to the full experience. At home he could sometimes be seen sitting rigidly when helicopters passed overhead or when neighborhood noise unexpectedly snapped sharp and loud outside the window. In those moments his face would change, not with drama but with a tightening that made him look older, as though he were bracing for blame. The consequences reached beyond his own mind: he became less available, more irritable, and less willing to join social plans, because he did not trust what might be triggered by a busy restaurant, a televised report, or even the sound of people shouting over one another. He hated that his relationship had begun to feel shaped by what he could not bear to discuss. Still, whenever the memory came back, the old appraisal followed immediately behind it, and whenever he judged himself harshly, the memory seemed to come back more vividly, as if guilt itself were pulling him back into the street.

By the time he sought help, Rafael’s PCL-5 score reflected what had become a heavy, entrenched burden. He came because he was tired of living as if he were always one sound or image away from being thrown back into that scene, and because he was frightened that the numb stretches and the flooding guilt both meant he was becoming less himself. What he wanted most was to stop seeing that day as proof that he was a weak man who failed everyone around him, and what frightened him most was the possibility that he would spend the rest of his life carrying the same unforgivable memory, vivid one moment and empty the next, without ever being able to set it down.
